## Today 

- Have a look at some R-package-dev practices.

- We won’t discuss either Rcpp or coding R itself. (for that I recommend ["Advance R"](http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Rcpp.html), and there’s also Patrick Muchmore’s ["A template for R packages using Rcpp and/or RcppArmadillo"](https://github.com/patrickmuchmore/RPackageTemplate))

- We won’t discuss GitHub in depth. I’ll assume that the user already knows the basics of Git(Hub): Creating a repo online and start using it locally. (A good reference is ["Pro Git"](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) and ["Happy Git and GitHub for the useR"](https://happygitwithr.com/))

- We won’t discuss software engineering/design; we’ll look at some tools and dev cycles. (For that, you have ["CodeComplete"](http://cc2e.com/))


## What we’ll be using today

1.  **devtools**: "Package development tools for R" ([read more](https://cran.r-project.org/package=devtools)).

2.  **roxygen2**: "A ‘Doxygen’-like in-source documentation system for Rd, collation, and ‘NAMESPACE’ files" ([read more](https://cran.r-project.org/package=roxygen2)).

3.  **covr**: (An R package for) "Test Coverage for Packages" ([read more](https://cran.r-project.org/package=covr)).

4.  **RStudio**: "RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R" ([read more](https://cran.r-project.org/package=covr)).

5.  **valgrind**: (if you use C/C++ code) "a memory error detector" ([read more](http://valgrind.org/)).


## Why 'spend' time writing an R package?


To name a few:

1. Easy way to share code: Type `install.packages` and voila!

2. Already standardized: So you don't need to think about how to structure it.

3. CRAN checks everything for you: Force yourself to code things right.

4.  **Reproducible Research**
    
    - Accessible Reproducible Research ([Mesirov, **Science** 2010](http://science.sciencemag.org/content/327/5964/415))
  
    - Again, and Again, and Again, ... ([Jasny et al., **Science** 2011](http://science.sciencemag.org/content/334/6060/1225))
  
    - Challenges in Irreproducible Research ([**nature** topic](http://www.nature.com/news/reproducibility-1.17552))


## Not so obvious examples

- **Implementing a pipeline**: A collection of functions that are used to process data in a specific way. *e.g.*, CDC's epinow2-pipeline ([link](https://github.com/CDCgov/cfa-epinow2-pipeline)). 

- **Branding**: You can create an extension for `Rmarkdown`, `quarto`, or `ggplot2` (to name a few) that contains your company’s colors and logos. e.g., University of Southern California's IMAGE grant ([link](https://github.com/USCbiostats/uscimage)) (see also [this](https://quarto.org/docs/extensions/formats.html) for quarto formats.)

- **Shiny apps**: So it is easier to share them with other users, *e.g.*, the [`epiworldRShiny`](https://github.com/UofUEpiBio/epiworldRShiny) implements a shiny-version of the [`epiworldR`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=epiworldR) R package. 

- **Sharing Data**: There are multiple R packages that only contain data, for instance, the `gapminder` package ([link](https://cran.r-project.org/package=gapminder)).



## What’s an R package, anyway?

According to Hadley Wickham’s ["R packages"](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/)

> Packages are **the fundamental units of reproducible R code**. They include **reusable R functions**, the **documentation** that describes how to use them, and **sample data**.


## What’s an R package, anyway? (cont.) 

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

Folders

  - **R** Where the R scripts live, e.g., `addnums.r`, `boring-pkg.r`.

  - **tests** Where the tests live, e.g., `testthat/test-addnums.r`
    (using [testthat](https://cran.r-project.org/package=testthat) or [tinytest](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tinytest)).

  - **vignettes** Where vignettes live, e.g.,
    `vignettes/mode_details_on_addnums.rmd`.

  - **data** Where the data lives, e.g., `fakedata.rda`,
    `aneattable.csv`.

  - **man** Where the manuals live, e.g., `addnums.Rd`, `boringpkg.Rd`.

And files

  - **DESCRIPTION** The metadata of the package: name, description,
    version, author(s), dependencies, etc.

  - **NAMESPACE** Declares the name of the objects (functions mainly)
    that will be part of the package (and will be visible to the user)

More info [here](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/package.html) and
[here](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Package-structure)

:::


## Dev cycle

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

Writing R packages is an iterative process

1.  **Set up the structure**: Create folders and files `R/`, `data/`,
    `src/`, `tests/`, `man/`, `vignettes/`, `DESCRIPTION`,
    `NAMESPACE`(?)

2.  **Code\!** For `f` in `F` do
    
    1.  Write `f`
    
    2.  Document `f`: what it does, what the inputs are, what it
        returns, and examples.
    
    3.  Add some tests: is it doing what it is supposed to do?
    
    4.  `R CMD Check`: Will CRAN and the rest of the functions ‘like’
        it?
    
    5.  Commit your changes\!: Update `ChangeLog`+`news.md`, and commit
        (so GitHub Actions runs)\!
    
    6.  next `f`

3.  Submit your package to CRAN/Bioconductor (read
    [more](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/release.html#release-submission))

:::

# Handson

## Step 1: Set up the structure

You have several methods: `package.skeleton()`, Rstudio’s "New Project",
`devtools::new()`, etc. You can also use `usethis::create_package()`.

```{r}
#| label: Creating-a-package
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
library(usethis)

# I'm using a temp folder, but you should use something else like
# "C:/Users/vegayon/Documents/boringpkg"
tmp_folder <- tempfile("boringpkg") 

# Creating the package
usethis::create_package(
  path = tmp_folder,
  roxygen = TRUE,   # Docs and NAMESPACE are generated from roxygen2 comments
  rstudio = TRUE,   # Adds an .Rproj file so you can open it as an RStudio project
  fields = list(    # Values written to the DESCRIPTION file
    Package = "boringpkg",
    Version = "0.0.0.9000",
    Title = "A boring package",
    Description = "A boring package"
  )
)

# We can inspect what things it created:
list.files(tmp_folder, recursive = TRUE)
```

Try it out!

## Step 1: Set up the structure (cont. 1)


And, using the `usethis` package, we can add some extras. Locally:

```r
# Creating a README for the project
usethis::use_readme_rmd()

# Infrastructure for testing
usethis::use_testthat()

# A LICENSE file (required by CRAN)
# The line "license: MIT + file" in the DESCRIPTION file
usethis::use_mit_license(copyright_holder = "George G. Vega Yon")
usethis::use_news_md()
```

If you are planning to use GitHub, you can set up GitHub Actions. This is GitHub's built-in automation service: it runs scripts on GitHub's own machines whenever something happens in your repo, such as a push. This setup is often called continuous integration (CI). For this to work, your package first needs to be a Git repository that is connected to GitHub.

```r
# Turn the package folder into a Git repository
usethis::use_git()

# Create a matching repo on GitHub and push to it
# (needs a GitHub token, see usethis::create_github_token())
usethis::use_github()

# Some basic CI infrastructure
usethis::use_github_action("check-standard")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Prefer the command line? Doing the Git setup with `git`

From a terminal inside the package folder, this does the same as `use_git()`:

```shell
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
```

For `use_github()`, first create an empty repo on [github.com](https://github.com/new) with the same name as your package (don't add a README or license, since you already have them). Then connect it and push:

```shell
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/boringpkg.git
git push -u origin main
```

If you have the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) installed, `gh repo create boringpkg --public --source=. --push` creates the repo and pushes in one step.
:::

Try it out! Other things we are not setting up: code coverage, which measures how much of your code your tests actually run (check out the `usethis::use_coverage()` function).

## Step 1: Set up the structure (cont. 2)

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

What did happen?

1. `use_readme_rmd()`: Creates a `README.Rmd` file in the project's main folder. Think about it as the home page of your project. You edit the `.Rmd` and knit it into `README.md`, which is what GitHub shows on the repo page. Since it can run R code, you can include working examples.

2. `use_testthat()`: Sets up the testing infrastructure. It creates the `tests/testthat/` folder (your test files go there) and `tests/testthat.R` (the script `R CMD check` uses to run them), and adds `testthat` to `Suggests` in `DESCRIPTION`.

3. `use_mit_license(copyright_holder = "George G. Vega Yon")`: Creates the `LICENSE` file and puts it under ‘George G. Vega Yon’. It also sets `License: MIT + file LICENSE` in `DESCRIPTION`. Without a license, others can't legally reuse your code.

4.  `use_news_md()`: Creates the `NEWS.md` file, which is used for tracking changes and communicating them to the users (e.g. [netdiffuseR](https://github.com/USCCANA/netdiffuseR/blob/master/NEWS.md)). Add a short entry every time you release a new version.

5. `use_git()` and `use_github()`: `use_git()` initializes a Git repository in the package folder and offers to make a first commit. `use_github()` creates a repo with the same name on your GitHub account, connects it to your local one, and pushes your files. It needs a personal access token: run `usethis::create_github_token()` to make one and `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()` to store it (see [Happy Git](https://happygitwithr.com/https-pat) for details).

6. `use_github_action("check-standard")`: Adds the workflow file `.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml`. Every time you push to GitHub (or open a pull request), GitHub runs `R CMD check` on macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu with the release and development versions of R. You can see the results in the **Actions** tab of your repo. This is how you find out your package breaks on Windows before CRAN tells you. Remember to commit and push the new workflow file, since GitHub only sees what you've pushed.

Now that we have the structure, we can start coding!

:::



## Step 2.1 and 2.2: Write `f` and Document it

::: {.columns style="font-size: 20pt"}

::: {.column width="40%"}

- Using `roxygen2` is very straight forward. For our fist pice of
    code, we create the `R/addnums.r` file (right).

- Type `devtools::document()`, or press Ctrl + Shift + D (RStudio
    will: create the manual and the NAMESPACE). Make sure you activate
    this option in RStudio (not the default).

- Notice that the output is defined using S3-type objects ([read
    more](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/s3.html))

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

  
    
```r
#' The title of -addnums-
#'
#' Here is a brief description
#' 
#' @param a Numeric scalar. A brief description.
#' @param b Numeric scalar. A brief description.
#' 
#' @details Computes the sum of \code{x} and \code{y}.
#' @return A list of class \code{boringpkg_addnums}:
#' \item{a}{Numeric scalar.}
#' \item{b}{Numeric scalar.}
#' \item{ab}{Numeric scalar. the sum of \code{a} and \code{b}}
#' @examples
#' foo(1, 2)
#' 
#' @export
addnums <- function(a, b) {
    ans <- a + b
    structure(list(a = a, b = b, ab = ans)
    , class = "boringpkg_addnums")
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does `devtools::document()` do?

It runs `roxygen2` on the `#'` comments in your `R/` files and writes two things from them:

1. **`man/*.Rd` files**: the help pages behind `?addnums`. Tags like `@param`, `@return`, and `@examples` become sections of the page. Don't edit these by hand, since the next `document()` overwrites them.

2. **The `NAMESPACE` file**: `@export` becomes `export(addnums)`, so users can call the function. `@importFrom graphics axis` becomes `importFrom(graphics, axis)`.

Run it again every time you change a roxygen comment, otherwise the help pages and `NAMESPACE` fall out of date. Note that it does not touch `Imports` in `DESCRIPTION`. You add those yourself, e.g., with `usethis::use_package("graphics")`.
:::

## Detour: Why use S3 in a package?

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

`addnums()` returns a list with a class attribute. This is S3, the object system used by most of base R and CRAN, and it has several advantages:

- **Users already know the functions:** If your output has a class, users can call `print()`, `summary()`, or `plot()` on it, just like they do with the output of `lm()`.

- **Results stay together:** A classed list keeps the inputs and the result in one object. `addnums()` returns `a`, `b`, and `ab` together.

- **Others can extend it:** Another package can add a method for your class without changing your code.

- **It's lightweight:** Turning a list into an S3 object takes one line, `class(x) <- "boringpkg_addnums"`. In S4 or S7, you first have to declare the class and the type of each field before you can create an object.

R also has other object systems. **S4** is more formal and is used throughout Bioconductor. **R6** gives objects that can be modified in place. **S7** is the newest one, built by the R Consortium as a successor to S3 and S4. S7 objects are also S3 objects, so what you learn here carries over.

Read more in the [S3 chapter](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/s3.html) of Hadley Wickham's *Advanced R*.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## More information on S7

For a long time, R package authors had two main choices. S3 is simple but informal: there is no way to say which fields an object should have, so it's easy to create broken objects. S4 fixes that, but it's verbose and harder to learn. Having two systems also split the community, with most of CRAN using S3 and Bioconductor using S4.

S7 was developed by the R Consortium's object-oriented programming working group, which includes members of R Core, Bioconductor, and the tidyverse team. The goal was a single system that keeps the simplicity of S3, adds the formal class definitions and validation of S4, and works with existing S3 and S4 code. The long-term plan is to include it in base R.

S7 classes are defined up front, with typed properties. Properties are accessed with `@`.

```r
library(S7)

addnums <- new_class("addnums", properties = list(
  a  = class_numeric,
  b  = class_numeric,
  ab = new_property(class_numeric, getter = function(self) self@a + self@b)
))

x <- addnums(a = 1, b = 2)
x@ab
#> [1] 3

# Methods are registered with method()
method(print, addnums) <- function(x, ...) cat(x@a, "+", x@b, "=", x@ab, "\n")
x
#> 1 + 2 = 3
```

Passing `a = "one"` gives an error, since `a` must be numeric. With S3, nothing stops you from creating a broken object.

**So should you use S7?** For most packages, S3 is still the default. It's part of base R, most packages you'll read use it, and tools like roxygen2 are built around it. S7 is still a separate package (not yet 1.0), so using it adds a dependency. Consider S7 when your objects have many fields that need checking, or when a method should depend on more than one argument. It is already used in production: ggplot2 4.0 moved its internals to S7.

See the [S7 documentation](https://rconsortium.github.io/S7/) for more.
:::

## Detour: S3 classes

Here we are leveraging S3 classes. In R, the S3 is a simple way to do object oriented programming. The way it works:

1. Objects should have a class attribute (e.g., `class(x) <- "myclass"`).

2. You can then define "methods" for that class, e.g., `print.myclass` and
`plot.myclass`.

3. These are valid as long as there is a generic function (e.g., `print` and `plot`) that can handle the class.

You can inspect the methods using the `methods()` function, e.g.,

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: showing-methods
#| code-overflow: scroll
#| echo: true
methods(generic.function = "print")
```
::: 

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: showing-methods-2
#| code-overflow: scroll
#| echo: true
methods(class = "glm")
```
:::
:::

## Detour: S3 classes (cont.)

You can also define your own methods, e.g.,:

```{r}
#| label: defining-methods
#| echo: true
my_generic <- function(x) UseMethod("my_generic")
my_generic.default <- function(x) "I don't know how to handle this"
my_generic.numeric <- function(x) "I know how to handle this"

my_generic("a")
my_generic(1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## S3 inside a package

- **Exporting methods:** Put `@export` above a method like `plot.boringpkg_addnums()`. When you run `devtools::document()`, roxygen sees that it is a method for the `plot` generic and writes `S3method(plot, boringpkg_addnums)` to `NAMESPACE`. Without this, calling `plot()` on your object from outside the package won't use your method, and `R CMD check` will complain.

- **Constructors:** The usual pattern is one function that checks the inputs and then sets the class, so every object of your class has the same structure. `addnums()` is a simple version of this, using `structure(..., class = "boringpkg_addnums")`.

- **Naming:** Prefix your class names with the package name (`boringpkg_addnums`) so they don't clash with classes from other packages.
:::

## Step 2.1 and 2.2: Write `f` and Document it (cont. 1)

Here we are defining a method for `plot.boringpkg_addnums`. Notice that the `plot` function already has a generic method, which is why we only need to define the method for `boringpkg_addnums`.

```r
#' @rdname addnums
#' @export
#' @param x An object of class \code{boringpkg_addnums}.
#' @param y Ignored.
#' @param ... Further arguments passed to
#' \code{\link[graphics:plot.window]{plot.window}}.
plot.boringpkg_addnums <- function(x, y = NULL, ...) {
    graphics::plot.new()
    graphics::plot.window(xlim = range(unlist(c(0,x))), ylim = c(-.5,1))
    graphics::axis(1)
    with(x, graphics::segments(0, 1, ab, col = "blue", lwd=3))
    with(x, graphics::segments(0, 0, a, col = "green", lwd=3))
    with(x, graphics::segments(a, .5, a + b, col = "red", lwd=3))
    graphics::legend("bottom", col = c("blue", "green", "red"), 
            legend = c("a+b", "a", "b"), bty = "n", 
            ncol = 3, lty = 1, lwd=3)
}
```

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

  - Here, we are adding a function that is documented in `addnums`. The
    plot method (above).

  - You’ll need to update the `man/*Rd` every time that you add new
    roxygen content. Press Ctrl + Shift + D, and RStudio will do it
    for you (or enter `devtools::document()` which calls `roxygen2::roxygenize()`).

  - Notice that functions from foreign packages are called using the
    `::` operator (read more
    [here](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/ns-dblcolon.html)
    and [here](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/namespace.html)). Not a
    requirement, but makes the code easier to maintain (and less
    error-prone... because of R’s scoping rules).

:::

## Step 2.1 and 2.2: Write `f` and Document it (cont. 2)

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

Our plot method uses foreign functions (i.e., function from the `graphics` package), so we need to declare that dependency. We also add a help page for the package as a whole.

:::

::: {.columns style="font-size: 20pt"}

::: {.column width="50%"}

`R/boringpkg-package.R`

```r
#' boringpkg
#'
#' A (not so) boring collection of functions
#'
#' @description We add stuff up... You can access the project
#' website at \url{https://github.com/USCbiostats/software-dev/tree/master/rpkgs/boringpkg}
#'
#' @author George G. Vega Yon
#' @keywords internal
"_PACKAGE"

## usethis namespace: start
#' @importFrom graphics axis legend plot.new plot.window segments
## usethis namespace: end
NULL
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

`DESCRIPTION`

```yml
Package: boringpkg
Type: Package
Title: What the Package Does (Title Case)
Version: 0.1.0
Author: Who wrote it
Maintainer: The package maintainer <yourself@somewhere.net>
Description: More about what it does (maybe more than one line)
    Use four spaces when indenting paragraphs within the Description.
License: What license is it under?
Encoding: UTF-8
LazyData: true
Suggests:
    testthat,
    covr
RoxygenNote: 5.0.1
Imports: graphics
```


:::

:::

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

- `usethis::use_package_doc()` creates this file. `"_PACKAGE"` tells roxygen to build the `?boringpkg` help page, an overview of the whole package. By default, it fills in the title, description, and authors from `DESCRIPTION`. You can write your own text above `"_PACKAGE"`, as we do here, to give users a longer overview or a link to the project website. `@keywords internal` keeps this page out of the list of functions in the help index.

- The `usethis namespace` section holds imports for the whole package. `usethis::use_import_from("graphics", "axis")` adds tags there for you. The `NULL` at the end is needed because a roxygen block has to sit above an object.

- `usethis::use_package("graphics")` adds `graphics` to `Imports` in `DESCRIPTION`. Every package your code uses must be listed there, or `R CMD check` will complain. The `Suggests` and `RoxygenNote` fields were added automagically by `devtools`.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## `@importFrom` or `pkg::fun()`?

There are two ways to use a function from another package:

- **`graphics::axis()`**: you call it with the package name in front. No import is needed, only the `Imports` entry in `DESCRIPTION`. It's always clear where the function comes from.

- **`@importFrom graphics axis`**: you can then write `axis()` directly. This is handy for functions you use a lot, or ones that are awkward to write with `::`, like the pipe `%>%` from `magrittr`.

Our plot method uses `graphics::` everywhere, so strictly the `@importFrom` line isn't needed here. We show it so you know what it looks like. In your own package, pick one style and stick with it.

You may also see older packages document themselves with `@docType package` and `@name boringpkg` above a `NULL`. That still works, but `"_PACKAGE"` is the current recommended way.
:::

## Step 2.3: Add some tests

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

Test are run every time that you run R CMD check

  - In the `tests/testthat/` dir, add/edit a source file with tests,
    e.g. `test-addnums.r`
    
    ```r
    test_that("addnums(a, b) = a+b", {
      # Preparing the test
      a <- 1
      b <- -2
    
      # Calling the function
      ans0 <- a+b
      ans1 <- addnums(a, b)
    
      # Are these equal?
      expect_equal(ans0, ans1$ab)
    })
    
    test_that("Plot returns -boringpkg_foo-", {
      expect_s3_class(
        plot(addnums(1,2)), "boringpkg_foo"
        ) # This will generate an error as the function plot.boringpkg_addnum
          # does not return an object of that class.
    })
    ```
  - You can run the tests using Ctrl + Shift + t

  - Furthermore, tests are used to evaluate code coverage.

:::

## Step 2.4: R CMD check

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

`R CMD check` is R's built-in tool for testing a whole package. It builds and installs the package, then runs a long list of checks: whether the `DESCRIPTION` is valid, whether every exported function is documented, whether the examples run, whether the tests pass, and whether the code uses packages it doesn't declare. It reports back errors, warnings, and notes. CRAN runs the same checks on every submission, so a clean check locally is the first thing to aim for. From R, `devtools::check()` runs it for you.

Running `R CMD check` is easy with RStudio

  - If you don’t have C/C++ code Just press Ctrl + Shift + E

  - If you have C/C++ code, use `R CMD Check` with valgrind (check for
    segfaults)
    
    ```shell
    $ R CMD build boringpkg/
    $ R CMD check --as-cran --use-valgrind boringpkg*.tar.gz
    ```
    
    You can ask RStudio to use valgrind too.

For an extensive list of the checks, see the section [1.3.1 Checking packages](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Checking-packages) in the "Writing R extensions" manual.


What does the output of `R CMD check` looks like?

```shell
==> devtools::check()

Updating boringpkg documentation
Loading boringpkg
Setting env vars ---------------------------------------------------------------
CFLAGS  : -Wall -pedantic
CXXFLAGS: -Wall -pedantic
Building boringpkg --------------------------------------------------------------
'/usr/lib/R/bin/R' --no-site-file --no-environ --no-save --no-restore --quiet  \
  CMD build  \
```

## Step 2.4: R CMD check (cont. 1)

::: {style="font-size: 25pt"}

R packages can be shared by "building" them. For example, the following
command:

```shell
R CMD build ~/Documents/boringpkg
```

Will generate package the R package into a file named `boringpkg_0.1.0.tar.gz` that
can later be distributed. Users can install this package either through command line:

```shell
R CMD INSTALL boringpkg_0.1.0.tar.gz
```

Or through the console in R

```r
install.packages("boringpkg_0.1.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL)
```

:::

## Step 2.5: Commit your changes

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

Once you have run R CMD checks and no errors or unexpected issues are
detected, you should commit your changes and push them to Github.

1.  Edit the
    [`NEWS.md`](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/NEWS.md)
    file and the
    [`ChangeLog`](https://github.com/RcppCore/RcppArmadillo/blob/master/ChangeLog)
    (if you have one).

    `NEWS.md` is a changelog written for your users. It lists what changed in each version: new functions, bug fixes, and changes that might break their code. Each version gets a heading, and each change gets a short bullet:

    ```markdown
    # boringpkg (development version)

    * New `plot()` method for `addnums()` output.

    # boringpkg 0.1.0

    * Initial release.
    ```

    CRAN shows this file on your package's page, and users can read it from R with `news(package = "boringpkg")`. It's easiest to add a bullet every time you make a change, so it's ready when you release.

2.  Add the new files to the tree, commit your changes, and push them to
    Github
    
    ```shell
    $ git add R/newfile.r man/newfile.Rd
    $ git commit -a -m "Adding new function"
    $ git push
    ```

Once uploaded, check the **Actions** tab of your GitHub repo to see if
`R CMD check` passed on all operating systems.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What about Travis CI and AppVeyor?

Older packages and tutorials mention Travis CI and AppVeyor. These were CI services that did the same job before GitHub Actions existed: Travis for Linux and macOS, AppVeyor for Windows. Around 2020 to 2021, Travis stopped offering its free plan for open-source projects. Most R packages then moved to GitHub Actions, which is free for public repos, runs on all three operating systems, and is set up with a single `usethis` call.
:::

:::

## Step 3: Submit your package to CRAN/Bioconductor

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

These are the two main places where R users get packages:

  - **CRAN** (the Comprehensive R Archive Network) is R's official package repository. When someone runs `install.packages("boringpkg")`, this is where the package comes from. It hosts packages from every field. Submissions are reviewed by volunteers, and your package has to pass `R CMD check` on several operating systems. After acceptance, CRAN keeps checking it as R and other packages change, and may remove it if it starts failing.

  - **Bioconductor** is a repository for packages that analyze biological data, mostly genomics. Users install from it with `BiocManager::install()`. Each submission gets a code review from a Bioconductor team member, it must include a vignette, and it should reuse Bioconductor's existing data structures where possible. New versions come out twice a year.

If your package isn't about biological data, CRAN is the usual choice.

To submit to CRAN:

  1. Run `usethis::use_release_issue()`. It opens a GitHub issue with a checklist of everything to do before a release (see the box below).

  2. Work through the checklist.

  3. Run `devtools::submit_cran()`. It builds the package and uploads it to CRAN. CRAN then emails you a link to confirm the submission.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Before you submit to CRAN

1. `devtools::check()` locally: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Explain any notes in `cran-comments.md` (create it with `usethis::use_cran_comments()`).
2. `devtools::check_win_devel()`: checks your package on CRAN's Windows machine with the development version of R. Results arrive by email.
3. The GitHub Actions check passes on all operating systems.
4. Update the version number (`usethis::use_version()`) and `NEWS.md`.

These are the main items on the `use_release_issue()` checklist. After you submit, CRAN runs its own automatic checks, and then a volunteer reviews the package.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What about `devtools::release()`?

For many years, `devtools::release()` was the standard way to submit. It asked you a series of yes/no questions (Did you run `R CMD check`? Did you update `NEWS.md`?) and then submitted the package. Hadley Wickham, the author of devtools, was so confident in it that its help page came with a warranty:

> If a devtools bug causes one of the CRAN maintainers to **treat
> you impolitely**, I will personally send you a handwritten apology
> note. Please forward me the email and your address, and I’ll get a
> card in the mail.

`release()` is now deprecated. The devtools team no longer uses it themselves, so they can't promise it follows current best practices. The checklist from `use_release_issue()` replaces the questions, and `submit_cran()` does the uploading. You will still see `release()` in older tutorials.
:::

## Dev Cycle (once again\!)

::: {style="font-size: 20pt"}

The most important step

2.  **Code\!** For `f` in `F` do
    
    1.  Write `f`
    
    2.  Document `f`: what it does, what the inputs are, what it
        returns, examples.
    
    3.  Add some tests: is it doing what is supposed to do?
    
    4.  `R CMD Check`: Will CRAN, and the rest of the functions, ‘like’
        it?
    
    5.  Commit your changes\!: Update `ChangeLog`+`news.md`, and commit
        (so GitHub Actions runs)\!
    
    6.  next `f`


:::
